definitions.definition: A structural similarity between two different systems where the parts correspond in a way that preserves relationships.
definitions.example: A map of a subway system is isomorphic to the actual tracks because the connections between stations are the same, even though the map is not the same size or shape.

definitions.definition: A sequence of frequencies that are whole-number multiples of a base frequency, which forms the basis of musical sound.
definitions.example: If you pluck a guitar string, the main note is the fundamental, but it also produces quieter higher notes (overtones) at 2x, 3x, 4x the frequency, which together make the harmonic series.

definitions.definition: A pleasant, stable sound created when two or more notes have simple frequency ratios.
definitions.example: Playing a C and a G together sounds nice because their frequencies are in a simple 3:2 ratio.

definitions.definition: An unstable, tense sound created when two or more notes have complex frequency ratios.
definitions.example: Playing a C and an F# together sounds harsh because their frequencies are in a complex 45:32 ratio.

definitions.definition: The tendency of musical notes to be attracted toward a central note (the tonic), like gravity pulling objects toward Earth.
definitions.example: In a song in C major, all the notes feel like they want to return to the note C, especially at the end.

definitions.definition: The lowest and most dominant frequency of a sound, which determines the pitch you hear.
definitions.example: When you play an A on a piano, the fundamental frequency is 440 Hz, and that's the note you recognize.

definitions.definition: The interval between one musical pitch and another with double its frequency, sounding like the same note but higher.
definitions.example: When you play a middle C and then the next C up on a piano, that's an octave.

definitions.definition: A musical interval with a frequency ratio of 3:2, which sounds very stable and pleasant.
definitions.example: The first two notes of 'Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star' are a perfect fifth apart.

definitions.definition: A mathematical formula created by Leonhard Euler to measure how pleasant a musical interval sounds based on the simplicity of its frequency ratio.
definitions.example: Euler's formula would give a high score (pleasant) to a simple ratio like 2:1 and a low score (unpleasant) to a complex ratio like 45:32.

definitions.definition: A measure of how harsh or rough a sound feels to the ear, caused by rapid beating between close frequencies.
definitions.example: When two notes are very close in pitch, they create a wobbly, rough sound, and Helmholtz's function calculates how rough that is.

definitions.definition: Graphs that show how dissonance changes as two tones get closer or farther apart in frequency, based on how the ear processes sound.
definitions.example: These curves show that two notes very close together sound rough, but as they move apart, they become more consonant until they get too far and become dissonant again.

definitions.definition: A formal model that maps the distances between musical pitches, chords, and keys, explaining why some notes feel closer to the tonic than others.
definitions.example: In this model, the note G is closer to the tonic C than the note F# is, which is why G feels more attracted to C.

definitions.definition: The central note or chord of a musical key, which feels like home and where the music wants to resolve.
definitions.example: In the key of C major, the note C is the tonic, and songs often end on a C chord to feel finished.

definitions.definition: A four-note chord built on the fifth note of a scale that creates strong tension and wants to resolve to the tonic chord.
definitions.example: In the key of C, the G7 chord (G, B, D, F) sounds unstable and strongly pulls toward the C chord.

definitions.definition: A musical interval spanning three whole tones, which sounds very dissonant and unstable.
definitions.example: The interval between C and F# is a tritone, and it was historically called 'the devil's interval' because it sounds so harsh.

definitions.definition: A musical system based on a seven-note scale with a specific pattern of whole and half steps, like the major and minor scales.
definitions.example: The white keys on a piano from C to C form a diatonic scale (C major).

definitions.definition: A three-note chord consisting of a root, a third, and a fifth, which is the basic building block of harmony.
definitions.example: A C major triad is made of the notes C, E, and G.

definitions.definition: The Christian doctrine that God is one being existing as three distinct persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
definitions.example: The Trinity is like a single source of light that shines through three different colored filters, each showing a different aspect but all coming from the same light.

definitions.definition: The theological concept that God the Son (Jesus) has always existed and was 'begotten' or generated from God the Father, not created at a point in time.
definitions.example: The Son is like light coming from the sun—the light has always existed with the sun, not made later.

definitions.definition: The theological concept that the Holy Spirit has always existed and 'proceeds' or comes from the Father (and the Son), not created at a point in time.
definitions.example: The Spirit is like heat radiating from a fire—it has always come from the fire, not made separately.

definitions.definition: A formal statement of Christian beliefs, written in the 4th century, that defines the Trinity and the nature of Jesus.
definitions.example: The Nicene Creed is recited in many churches and says Jesus is 'begotten, not made, of one being with the Father.'

definitions.definition: A theoretical field in the Theophysics framework that represents the ordering, unifying influence that draws things toward harmony and away from disorder.
definitions.example: The coherence field is like a magnetic field that aligns scattered iron filings into a neat pattern.

definitions.definition: A principle in the Theophysics framework stating that all things are drawn toward their source or toward greater coherence, like gravity pulling objects toward Earth.
definitions.example: Just as a ball rolls downhill toward the lowest point, all created things are attracted toward their divine source.

definitions.definition: A mathematical equation saying that the divergence of the coherence field is zero, meaning the field does not spread out or degrade over time.
definitions.example: Think of a river that flows without losing any water to evaporation—the amount of water stays constant.

definitions.definition: The strength of connection or interaction between two systems or between a system and a field.
definitions.example: Two magnets have strong coupling when they are close together, and weak coupling when they are far apart.

definitions.definition: The study of how things are connected or arranged, focusing on relationships rather than exact measurements.
definitions.example: A donut and a coffee cup have the same topology because they both have one hole, even though they look different.

definitions.definition: A belief that God exists as only two persons (usually Father and Son), rejecting the Holy Spirit as a distinct person.
definitions.example: Binitarianism is like trying to make a chord with only two notes—it's incomplete and lacks the full harmony.

definitions.definition: The study of the Holy Spirit in Christian theology.
definitions.example: Pneumatology asks questions like 'Who is the Holy Spirit?' and 'What does the Spirit do?'

definitions.definition: A belief that God consists of four persons or aspects, which is considered heretical in mainstream Christianity.
definitions.example: Quaternity would be like adding a fourth note to a basic three-note chord—it's redundant and unnecessary.

definitions.definition: Relating to the study of the church, its nature, structure, and practices.
definitions.example: Ecclesiological questions include 'What is the purpose of the church?' and 'How should the church be organized?'

definitions.definition: Music that lacks a tonal center or key, deliberately avoiding the pull of tonal gravity.
definitions.example: Atonal music sounds chaotic and unpredictable because no note feels like home.

definitions.definition: Able to be proven wrong by evidence or experiment, which is a key requirement for a scientific theory.
definitions.example: The claim 'all swans are white' is falsifiable because finding one black swan would prove it wrong.

definitions.definition: The rules and patterns for how individual musical notes move from one chord to the next in a smooth, logical way.
definitions.example: In voice-leading, a note that is part of a dissonant chord usually moves up or down by just one step to resolve to a consonant chord.

definitions.definition: The process of changing from one musical key to another within a piece of music.
definitions.example: A song might start in C major and then modulate to G major by using a chord that belongs to both keys.

definitions.definition: A principle in the Theophysics framework stating that certain truths or structures remain the same even when they are expressed in different forms or contexts.
definitions.example: The idea '2 + 2 = 4' is conserved whether you write it in English, Spanish, or as Roman numerals.

definitions.definition: A higher frequency that sounds along with the main note (fundamental) of a musical sound, part of the harmonic series.
definitions.example: When you play a low C on a cello, you can hear faint higher notes like the G above it, which are overtones.

definitions.definition: A Roman philosopher from the 6th century who wrote about music as a form of mathematical theology.
definitions.example: Boethius believed that music reflected the harmony of the universe and the divine order.

definitions.definition: A mathematical tool that breaks down a complex sound wave into its individual frequency components.
definitions.example: A Fourier transform can take the sound of a chord and show you exactly which notes are playing and how loud each one is.

definitions.definition: A musical scale with five notes per octave, common in many cultures around the world.
definitions.example: The black keys on a piano form a pentatonic scale, and many folk songs use it.

definitions.definition: A musical scale with seven notes per octave, like the major and minor scales.
definitions.example: The white keys on a piano from C to C form a heptatonic scale.

definitions.definition: A musical scale that uses all twelve notes in an octave, including both white and black keys on a piano.
definitions.example: Playing every key on a piano in order from C to the next C is a chromatic scale.

definitions.definition: Relating to the study of music from different cultures around the world.
definitions.example: Ethnomusicological research might compare the scales used in Indian classical music with those in African drumming.

definitions.definition: A basic statement or principle that is accepted as true without proof, used as a starting point for reasoning.
definitions.example: In geometry, 'a straight line is the shortest distance between two points' is an axiom.

definitions.definition: An early Christian theologian and philosopher from the 4th-5th century who wrote extensively about the Trinity.
definitions.example: Augustine compared the Trinity to the mind, the knowledge of the mind, and the love between them.

definitions.definition: A Latin phrase meaning 'On the Trinity,' the title of a major work by Augustine about the three persons of God.
definitions.example: In De Trinitate, Augustine explores how love requires a lover, a beloved, and the love itself.

definitions.definition: A Latin phrase meaning 'On Music,' a work by Boethius that connects music to mathematics and theology.
definitions.example: De Musica argues that musical harmony reflects the mathematical order of the universe.

definitions.definition: A Bible verse that describes Jesus as 'the image of the invisible God,' meaning he perfectly shows what God is like.
definitions.example: Just as a photograph perfectly captures a person's appearance, Jesus perfectly shows God's character.

definitions.definition: A Bible verse that says Jesus is 'the exact imprint of God's nature,' meaning he is a perfect copy of God's essence.
definitions.example: Like a stamp that leaves an exact impression in wax, Jesus is the exact representation of God.

definitions.definition: A Bible verse that says the Spirit of God 'hovered over the waters' at the beginning of creation, showing the Spirit as a dynamic, moving force.
definitions.example: The Spirit is like a bird hovering over its nest, ready to act and bring life.

definitions.definition: A Bible verse where Jesus says the Spirit 'blows where he wishes,' comparing the Spirit to the wind that moves freely and unpredictably.
definitions.example: You can't control the wind, and you can't control the Spirit—both move in their own way.

definitions.definition: A Bible verse that says 'all things were made through' Jesus, meaning everything in creation comes from him.
definitions.example: Jesus is like the source of a river from which all water flows.

definitions.definition: A Bible verse that says 'you were bought with a price,' meaning salvation cost Jesus his life and is not free in the sense of being without cost.
definitions.example: It's like someone paying a huge ransom to free a prisoner—the freedom is a gift, but it cost the rescuer dearly.
